extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers outlining novels (Save the Cat! users / novelists plotting act three)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for plotting the third act of a novel using Blake Snyder's Save the Cat! 15-beat framework, with concrete micro-beats for the five-part finale and the final image. Focuses on timing, scene counts, and the narrative purpose of each micro-beat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act three word count and scene count
rubrics_metrics.description: If the average novel is about 80,000 words and the end section is about 25% of that, the third act is roughly 20,000 words. With an average scene length around 1,500 words, you can plan for about 14 scenes in the final act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write scenes between 1,000 and 2,000 words (sweet spot ~1,500). Use these figures to plan pacing and how many beats will be single-scene vs multi-scene (the post maps the 3rd act to ~14 scenes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beats may be single-scene or multi-scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Some beats in the Save the Cat! method will be single-scene beats while others are going to be multi-scene beats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan which beats will occupy one scene and which will stretch across several. For example, the Finale is a multi-scene beat that occupies most of Act Three, while the Final Image is a single-scene beat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat #14: The Finale (80%-99%)
rubrics_metrics.description: The finale is a multi-scene beat in which you need to resolve all the problems created throughout the entire story and prove that the protagonist has changed because they learned the theme of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post recommends a five-part finale to break Act Three into manageable micro-beats. In the example plan of 14 scenes, the finale makes up 13 of those scenes. Use the five-part structure to ensure resolution, theme demonstration, and emotional payoff—don’t skimp on this section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finale — Part 1: Gathering the Team
rubrics_metrics.description: In this micro-beat the protagonist gathers help so they can execute the plan from the Break into Three beat. Gathering the team can mean people, tools, supplies, plans, or mending fences with allies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is preparation for the climactic moment. 'Gathering' can be literal (rounding up people) or metaphorical (collecting information, tools, or reconciling relationships). Examples: Katniss locating Peeta; Maddy searching her mother's files for evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finale — Part 2: Executing the Plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Now that the team/tools are gathered, the protagonist and allies execute the plan. The plan usually appears to be working in this micro-beat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary characters may have moments to shine or sacrifice themselves so the protagonist can face the climactic moment alone. These sacrifices should serve the protagonist's arc, demonstrating progress toward their new self. Examples: Katniss and Peeta defeating tributes; Maddy confronting her mother.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finale — Part 3: High Tower Surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Things seem to be going well until they aren’t — the protagonist realizes they've been led into a trap (literal or metaphorical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This micro-beat shows that the protagonist may have been naive or overconfident and provides one last obstacle/opportunity to prove their change. Apply it metaphorically for non-action genres. Examples: rule change in The Hunger Games; Maddy learning she lacks SCID but is still vulnerable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finale — Part 4: Dig Deep Down
rubrics_metrics.description: A mini-debate and reaction to the High Tower Surprise. The protagonist appears to have nothing left—no hope, plan, or tools—but still has what they learned throughout the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the emotional low where the protagonist must take a leap of faith and act from their new self. It’s the point readers have been waiting for to see the protagonist truly change. Example: Katniss deciding to rebel instead of simply surviving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finale — Part 5: Execution of the New Plan
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist puts their new, bold plan into action—this is the climax of the five-part finale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The new plan may succeed or fail; either is acceptable, but if the protagonist fails, the failure must have a clear purpose and lesson. This micro-beat should provide payoff for the character's growth (e.g., Katniss and Peeta's berry stunt; Maddy flying to find Olly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary-character sacrifices must serve protagonist growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Sacrifices by secondary characters should not be gratuitous; they exist to enable the protagonist to face the climactic moment alone and to highlight the protagonist’s growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a secondary character dies, is injured, or steps aside, ensure that act advances protagonist's arc and clarifies theme rather than just checking a plot box. Use these moments to deepen stakes and isolate the protagonist for the final test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat #15: The Final Image Beat (100%)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Final Image is a single-scene beat that shows readers an 'after' snapshot of the protagonist’s life and how much they have changed. It is the opposite of the Opening Image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the contrast with the opening image obvious—the farther apart opening and final images are, the clearer the story's point. This single final scene should visually/viscerally demonstrate the protagonist’s growth and the thematic conclusion (examples: Katniss and Peeta returned as victors but changed; Maddy's drawing and the book gift signaling her new life).
